episodes.201972: Southerly flow on the western side of high pressure centered over the south central U.S. resulted in higher moisture across eastern NM on June 21st. This higher moisture combined with daytime heating resulted in in the development of scattered thunderstorms across far eastern NM during the late afternoon hours eventually merging together into a line of storms near the Texas border during the evening hours. These storms brought a 58-mph wind gust to the Dora West Texas mesonet site and a 60 mph wind gust to Clovis Municipal Airport. Storms exited into West Texas around sunset.
episodes.202069: Heavy rainfall over a 3-4 hour period led to widespread flash and nuisance flooding across portions of Limestone and Madison Counties during the afternoon and early evening hours of the 22nd. Several roads were closed and numerous families had to be evacuated from their homes and apartments during the flooding in Harvest in Madison County, AL. 6-12 of water affected the apartments in Harvest, forcing residents to require assistance in leaving their homes during the event. No injuries or fatalities were reported.
episodes.202075: Outflow from a remnant Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) produced localized gale-force wind gusts over the upper Chesapeake Bay.
episodes.202099: A MCS (Mesoscale Convective System) traveled along the heat ridge across the eastern half of the CONUS across southern Canada and then moved southeast across the Lake Ontario region, including clipping southwest St. Lawrence county where thunderstorm winds in excess of 60 mph were observed.
episodes.202410: An early season plume of monsoon moisture advected northward into New Mexico from June 22nd through the 24th bringing several days of flash flooding and severe weather across portions of northern and central NM. June 22nd in particular saw severe thunderstorms produce numerous severe wind gusts of 60 mph or stronger across eastern NM from Roswell to Nara Visa with reports of downed utility poles and arcing powerlines near Roswell and dust being kicked up in Quay County. Heavy rains also produced flash flooding reports in Roswell where multiple cars and a fire truck were stuck in deep water. June 23rd saw thunderstorms bring burn scar flash flooding to the Ruidoso area burn scars where swift water rescues were performed at a mobile home park and a hotel. Flash flooding was also reported along an area where two to three inches or more of rain fell just south of I-40 in eastern NM near Santa Rosa and Newkirk. The Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon burn scar saw flash flooding on June 24th from burn scar flash flooding when NM 518 was closed due to flood waters. Heavy rains also produced flash flooding in Belen, NM where debris and high waters washed out a portion of I-25 at mile marker 190 which required cleanup crews to reopen the next day. Monsoon moisture began to lower after the 24th as did the thunderstorm activity by June 25th. ||Key Impacts: Flash flooding, burn scar flash flooding, debris flow, thunderstorm wind gust.
episodes.202657: During the evening of June 22nd, thunderstorms in New Mexico grew into a line of storms and moved into the western combined Panhandles. These storms formed in a fairly unstable environment and posed a severe threat in to the central to western combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. These storms produced severe wind gusts as several mesonet ground stations recorded severe wind gusts and even up to 65mph.
episodes.202943: Thunderstorms developed near the Wyoming and Nebraska border and quickly became severe as they moved into western Nebraska during the afternoon of June 22nd. Very large hail and wind gusts up to 70 mph were reported.
episodes.202945: A severe thunderstorm moved from northwest South Dakota into southwest North Dakota in an environment of modest instability but strong deep layer shear. The storm produced one-inch diameter hail in far southern Adams County.
episodes.203200: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) dropped southward across Central NY from eastern Ontario, moving into an environment with plenty of moisture and instability during the early morning hours. This complex of thunderstorms started to bow out and produced widespread damaging wind gusts and heavy rain.  A couple of small kinks along the leading edge of the line of storms did result in two EF-1 tornadoes spinning up before daybreak in Oneida County. Unfortunately one of the tornadoes resulted in 3 fatalities in Clark Mills, NY.
episodes.203248: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) dropped southward across Northeastern Pennsylvania moving into an environment with plenty of moisture and some instability during the late morning and early afternoon hours. While storms were non-severe, lightning was frequently observed. Two young men sustained minor injuries after being struck by lightning while working on a car.
episodes.203491: Thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon hours of June 22nd over Logan, northwestern Custer and Blaine Counties. This activity quickly intensified, becoming severe around 5 PM CDT over Blaine County. Activity persisted over the eastern Sandhills and portions of north central Nebraska into the mid evening hours. This activity produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter. Thunderstorm wind gusts, estimated at 80 MPH, broke a power pole and led to severe tree damage in southwestern Holt County. A second area of severe thunderstorms tracked into the northeastern Panhandle. Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 65 MPH were reported in Garden County.
episodes.203630: Late afternoon easterly flow sea breeze convection produces a pair of waterspouts off of Anna Maria Island near the mouth of Tampa Bay and gusty marine winds over Charlotte Harbor and Pine Island Sound waters.
episodes.203662: After a cool start to the month of June which slowed the melting of the mountain snowpack, Palmer quickly warmed up from June 10 through 21, 2025. In this timeframe, the Palmer airport reported six days of 70��F or above temperatures with a high of 75��F on June 19th. This reflects a warm and dry pattern that set up region-wide which enhanced snowmelt in the headwaters of the Matanuska River. Only 0.02 inches of rain fell at Palmer from June 10-21, but the warm weather caused rapid snowmelt and increased river flow as measured at the Matanuska River bridge (MATA2 Gage) in downtown Palmer during this period.||Weather throughout the region prior to the flooding of the Matanuska River featured a rapid change from cool and wet to warm and dry. Temperature measurements at the Palmer Airport indicate average temperature departures of up to 7.8��F below normal from June 1 to June 10 followed by a rapid increase in temperatures up to 4.8 degrees above normal from June 12 to June 21. Perhaps what is most notable, and the reason for rapid river rises along the Matanuska River, is the change in the alpine environment during this time period. For analysis, the Marmot Peak weather station located at 4,500 ft and the Independence Mine Snow Telemetry Site (SNOTEL) at 3,450 ft, both located in Hatcher Pass, will be used as proxy stations for the alpine and snow environment for the Matanuska River drainage. These stations are the only ones available in the region at representative elevations, and while neither of these stations directly influence the Matanuska River drainage, conditions were likely very similar.||Temperature data from the Marmot Peak weather station shows temperatures between June 1 and June 10 ranging from 26.1��F to 39.9��F with an average of 31.5��F. From June 11 to June 21, temperatures rose to between 35.6��F and 61.9��F with an average of 47.3��F. Analysis of the snow water equivalent shows little to no snow melt from June 1 to June 10 with multiple days of snow accumulation and a liquid equivalent increase up to 1 inch measured from June 6 to June 8. This was followed by a loss of 17.2 inches of liquid equivalent between June 10 and June 24. High resolution satellite imagery captured by the Sentinel-2 polar orbiting satellite shows a rapid reduction in high-elevation snowpack surrounding the greater Palmer area and Lower Matanuska Valley. Similar satellite imagery shows an altered river state from June 12 to June 20.
episodes.204095: A Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) developed in Ontario and tracked south into New York in the early morning hours on Sunday, June 22. This system eventually tracked through the Western Adirondacks into the western Mohawk Valley, inflicting fairly widespread wind damage across southern Herkimer County. Numerous reports were relayed to NWS Albany of tree and wire damage that ultimately led to the blockage and closure of numerous roadways. Trees were also reported down on sheds, fences, and even on a mobile home (in the town of Schuyler) but no injuries were reported.
episodes.204177: Scattered showers and thunderstorms impacted parts of East Texas during the afternoon hours on June 22nd as convection continued to develop and locally expand in coverage as a result of colliding outflow boundaries. In advance of the developing convection, a moist and unstable environment was in place, with MLCAPE values as high as 3000 to 4000 J/kg and precipitable water values nearing 2 inches. A few of these thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts with downed trees across parts of Gregg County, including near the East Texas Regional Airport.

A deadly pre-dawn tornado spun up at a kink in a line of severe thunderstorms in Clark Mills. Numerous trees were uprooted or snapped, with many of them on structures. Three homes were sliced or crushed by trees. Two residents were killed in one of the heavily-damaged homes, and a third fatality occurred on the crushed end of another residence. The tornado quickly became intense while traveling southwest |initially, and destroyed a historic grist mill along Oriskany Creek. The tornado then became absorbed into the southward motion of the line of thunderstorms, traveling along Kirkland Avenue before ending. While there was this focused corridor of convergent enhanced EF1 tornado damage, other scattered tree damage could be found throughout the area associated with damaging winds up to 70 mph from the line of severe storms.

A pre-dawn line of severe thunderstorms dropped south across the county. Rotation occurred in a kink in the line of storms, generating an EF1 tornado from just south of Westmoreland, through the western edge of the Hamilton College Campus, to near|Clinton. Numerous trees were uprooted or snapped, and a farm sustained significant damage to its silo and outbuildings. Debris from the farm was lofted at least 1000 feet across the field, with some of it impaling the ground as debris missiles. While there was this focused corridor of convergent enhanced EF1 tornado damage, other scattered tree damage could be found throughout the area associated with damaging winds up to 70 mph from the line of severe storms.
